<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qingni Wang<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Simular
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Changdae Oh
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Wisconsin–Madison
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuzhe Yang<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Simular
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sharon Li
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Wisconsin–Madison
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jiachen Yang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Simular
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ang Li
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Simular
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xin Eric Wang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Simular
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Weak-to-strong escalation</em> offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed.
The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor.
To this end, we propose <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em>, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent’s latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward.
<em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> has three layers:
(1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent.
Here, we use <em id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent uncertainty</em> as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model’s hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty.
During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training.
Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that <em id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, <em id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22280v1/frontier_qwen352.svg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/222;" width="405" height="222"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy–cost comparison between <em id="S0.F1.6.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> and random task-level routing on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The area spanned by random routing is obtained from repeated random task allocations across different escalation budgets; the band shows <math id="S0.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math> standard deviation over 10,000 allocations. At matched inference cost, <em id="S0.F1.6.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> achieves 9.1 percentage points higher task success.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate tasks of graphical interfaces by translating natural-language instructions and visual observations into executable actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon automation tasks that can take more than an hour on average <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abhyankar et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. While frontier proprietary models have been shown to achieve impressive performance leaps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026a</a>)</cite>, running every single task spanning hundreds of steps with these models raises cost concerns, whereas a light open-weight model alone performs poorly on even much simpler tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
This creates a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and cost efficiency, motivating <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weak-to-strong escalation</span> (W2SE), in which a weak agent serves as the primary executor and hands control to a strong agent only when needed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lei and Huang, 2026</a>)</cite>.
W2SE raises two important questions: (1) When should the weak agent escalate, and (2) who oversees the strong agent after handing over?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing work on W2SE primarily focuses on the first question, estimating the weak agent’s failure risk to decide when escalation is needed. Some of them adopt another monitoring agent to verify each step <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, others train an extra monitoring module on the collection of annotated trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lei and Huang, 2026</a>)</cite>. However, the former inevitably adds nontrivial cost to run another heavy agent step-by-step, whereas the latter creates another phase of data annotation and training, hindering direct adoption in real-world applications under varying deployment constraints. While training-free uncertainty estimation-based approaches might avoid the aforementioned bottlenecks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, prior works still rely on external knowledge base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, another reference model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, or multiple sampling for each step <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> quickly becomes infeasible or impractical in long-horizon tasks in the wild.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Besides, escalation alone does not eliminate execution uncertainty, resulting in the second important question in W2SE which is commonly overlooked. That is, even after a stronger agent takes control, subsequent actions may deviate from the intended task or fail to achieve the desired outcome. However, monitoring a black-box strong agent is challenging because its
internal states are inaccessible and verbalized confidence can be unreliable on evolving context of long-horizon task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchhof et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To answer both questions, we formulate W2SE as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, and use the weak agent’s failure risk as a proxy for the expected benefit of escalation. We then propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">L</span>atent uncertainty for <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E</span>scalation <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>nd <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SH</span>adow oversight (<em id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em>), a training-free framework driven by the uncertainty signal in the weak agent’s hidden states. First, we record its hidden states of prompt and action tokens on a small set of held-out tasks and label them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes to construct a representation bank. This representation bank then serves as a semantic anchor to score the newly faced prompts and actions during test-time by measuring, under a Mahalanobis metric in latent space, how much closer each one lies to past failures than to past successes.
<em id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> puts this signal on two jobs (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>): For <em id="S1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">escalation</em>, an initial gate scores uncertainty from the task prompt query, while a runtime gate monitors subsequent execution trace. For <em id="S1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">oversight</em>, after the weak model hands the control to the strong agent, it switches its role from actor to observer that monitors the strong agent’s trajectory every three steps; when its uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort.
Importantly, our uncertainty-driven W2SE formulation draws on an easily accessible resource, the weak agent’s own past experience <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silver and Sutton, 2025</a>)</cite>, removing reliance on an external dataset or additional training without hosting another expensive agent during runtime, while offering extensibility for recursive self-improvement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber, 2007</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> on OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with four open-weight weak agents and Claude Opus 5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026b</a>)</cite> as the strong agent. At matched escalation rates, <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points. We further measure how much of the performance gap between the weak agent alone and always-on Opus is recovered by escalation, following the performance-gap metric of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burns et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> recovers 75–102% of this gap, against 37–69% for random escalation, while costing 69–81% as much as always-on Opus. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite>, <em id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> matches always-on Opus (73.7% vs. 72.9% success) at 19% lower cost, whereas random escalation at equal cost scores about 9 points lower (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.22280v1/overview.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/166;" width="476" height="166" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of uncertainty-aware weak-to-strong escalation and post-handoff oversight. A weak agent goes through the task until its uncertainty scores trigger initial or step-level escalation; otherwise, the weak agent continues. After escalation is triggered, the strong agent retains control while the weak agent changes its role from an actor to a shadow observer for continued monitoring. The feedback path from weak observer to strong actor enables uncertainty-triggered reflection and intervention. In short, <em id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent’s latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem and show that one latent uncertainty signal can drive both escalation and oversight.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a training-free, scalable uncertainty scoring method that measures how much closer a hidden state lies to the weak agent’s own past failures than to its past successes, and provide theoretical justification for using this score for escalation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend this uncertainty signal to weak-to-strong oversight, in which the white-box weak agent monitors the black-box strong agent through its own hidden states.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On OSWorld with four open-weight backbones, we show that <em id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em> outperforms random escalation at matched escalation rates and recovers 75–102% of the escalation gap at 69–81% of the cost of using always strong agent.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficient Computer-Use Agents.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model routing and cascading offer a promising way to balance inference cost and performance, as demonstrated by FrugalGPT and RouteLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dekoninck et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Extending this idea to GUI automation, Adaptive VLM Routing selects models based on action difficulty and confidence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, while StepWise trains lightweight monitors to detect execution stalls and identify milestones for escalation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Our work instead leverages the backbone agent’s internal representations to guide both task-level routing and step-level escalation, without training a dedicated monitoring network.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weak-to-Strong Paradigms.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weak-to-strong generalization studies how stronger models learn from weaker supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burns et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Somerstep et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Medvedev et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jung et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These works primarily concern training-time transfer of supervision or capabilities from a weaker model to a stronger one.
Here we study the complementary inference-time setting of <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weak-to-strong escalation</em> (W2SE), where a weak model executes by default and selectively invokes a stronger model when additional capability is needed.
This shifts the weak–strong relationship from supervision transfer to sequential resource allocation. We derive escalation signals from the agent’s own past experience without training an additional monitor.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty Estimation and Agent Monitoring.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Uncertainty estimation of agentic systems has emerged as one of the most important problems to monitor and guide agent decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh et al., 2026b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chun et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, while SafeGround and Argus investigate uncertainty estimation for GUI grounding, including calibrated predictions and representation-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Sampling-based uncertainty estimation and risk control have also been studied for question answering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, but repeated generation can be costly when applied at every step of a long-horizon agent trajectory.
Meanwhile, another line of work explores weak-to-strong oversight of agent misbehavior and failure monitoring through observable trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greenblatt et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kale et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Rather than focusing on either escalation or oversight alone, we handle both problem in a single unified fueled by a simple uncertainty estimate. That is, we integrate representation-based uncertainty estimation into the execution workflow, reusing the backbone model’s hidden states for escalation and extending the same signal to post-handoff oversight of a closed-source strong agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LEASH</em>, a training-free uncertainty-driven agentic inference framework for W2SE and post-handoff oversight (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). By comparing the weak model’s runtime hidden states with successful and failed reference executions, we estimate uncertainty at task initialization and during execution, which guides both escalation to the strong agent and continued oversight after handoff. We first formulate the problem in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Method ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> and introduce each component in subsequent sections.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Formulation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a task query, a computer-use agent generates an action conditioned on the query, the screen, and history. We consider a lightweight, weak agent, e.g., a relatively small open-weight model with accessible hidden states, and a large, strong agent, e.g., a proprietary black-box frontier model, sharing a budget of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> actions. In addition to these two actor agents, we also host a Manager agent (with a strong model) who fires at the beginning to decompose the task and subsequently at subgoal boundaries to verify progress, constructing a minimal version of multi-agent workflow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agashe et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agashe et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Throughout execution, the Manager decomposes the task query into subgoals with screenshot-verifiable completion criteria and decides whether to advance, keep, or revise each subgoal (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). This decomposition naturally provides finer-grained supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chun and Russakovsky, 2026</a>)</cite>, allowing execution steps to inherit subgoal-level outcomes rather than relying solely on the final task-level label.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt the weak model as a starting agent for all tasks until control is transferred to the strong model by hitting some flags. Then, the strong model runs over the remaining action budget until the end of the task. Let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a task drawn from the task distribution, and let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> denote an escalation policy. For each task <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> induces a stopping time <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>esc</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>esc</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)=0</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the earliest escalation opportunity and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)=T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>esc</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)=T</annotation></semantics></math> denotes no escalation. Since the strong agent dominates per-step cost, we use the total escalation rate, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{esc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>esc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{esc}}</annotation></semantics></math>, as a budget proxy and want to maximize task success under limited budget:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[S^{\pi}(x)\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left(t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)&lt;T\right)\leq p_{\mathrm{esc}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>π</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.447em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>s.t.</mtext><mspace style="width:1.167em;" width="1.167em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>esc</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>esc</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[S^{\pi}(x)\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left(t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\pi}(x)&lt;T\right)\leq p_{\mathrm{esc}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:60%;"><img src="2610.22280v1/figures/uncertainty2.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/143;" width="286" height="143" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Construction of the query and action reference banks for latent space uncertainty estimation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{\pi}(x)\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{\pi}(x)\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates task success under escalation policy <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. That is, we want to run tasks and each step within them through the weak agent as many times as possible unless it fails, to minimize the cost while achieving a high task success rate, becoming a problem <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">when-to-escalate</span>. Unlike existing works that adopt other monitoring agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026</a>)</cite> incurring additional inference costs or training-based monitors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite> requiring annotation costs and an additional training phase, we propose to use simple uncertainty estimates as a signal to determine when-to-escalate, without inducing any training cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Reference-Based Latent Uncertainty Estimation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by well-established observations revealing that LLMs internalize the likelihood of task success or failure in their representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azaria and Mitchell, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kossen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al., 2025</a>)</cite> even before generating any tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cencerrado et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Afzal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we propose a training-free, representation-distance-based uncertainty estimation technique for agent systems.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Representations and reference banks.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each task from a small held-out set, we run a weak agent to collect some preliminary inference trajectories without escalating anything to a strong agent. During this inference over the held-out set, we extract two final-layer representations, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> at the last task query prompt token, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> at the last generated action token of each execution step <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. The former captures information over the instruction and initial screen before decoding, whereas the latter also incorporates the action executed by the agent.
These hidden states build representation banks pairing each hidden state with progress outcome:
The query bank <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{q}=\{(h_{i,0},y_{i})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{q}=\{(h_{i,0},y_{i})\}</annotation></semantics></math> adopts task outcomes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}\in\{\textup{{Pass}},\textup{{Fail}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Pass</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Fail</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}\in\{\textup{{Pass}},\textup{{Fail}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas the action bank <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{a}=\{(h_{i,t},y_{i,t})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{a}=\{(h_{i,t},y_{i,t})\}</annotation></semantics></math> assigns each step its corresponding subgoal segment’s outcome (assessed by a Manager agent):
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Pass</span> if the subgoal is successfully completed, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Fail</span> if it should be revised, and otherwise the final task outcome.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty score.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each channel of representation banks <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\{q,a\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\{q,a\}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., query and action, we fit a shared-covariance Gaussian discriminant model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mukhoti et al., 2023</a>)</cite> on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>. We first standardize each representation with the bank statistics, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{c}(h)=(h-\bar{h}_{c})/s_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{c}(h)=(h-\bar{h}_{c})/s_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{h}_{c},s_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{h}_{c},s_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> are the feature-wise mean and standard deviation of all hidden states in <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> (pooled over both outcomes) and the division is element-wise. Let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{c,y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{c,y}</annotation></semantics></math> be the centroid of the standardized representations in <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> with outcome <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{c,\lambda}=\widehat{\Sigma}_{c}+\lambda_{c}I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{c,\lambda}=\widehat{\Sigma}_{c}+\lambda_{c}I</annotation></semantics></math> the pooled within-class covariance regularized by <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{c}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{c}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. Using the squared Mahalanobis distance,</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{c,y}^{2}(h)=\bigl(z_{c}(h)-\mu_{c,y}\bigr)^{\top}\Sigma_{c,\lambda}^{-1}\bigl(z_{c}(h)-\mu_{c,y}\bigr)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{c,y}^{2}(h)=\bigl(z_{c}(h)-\mu_{c,y}\bigr)^{\top}\Sigma_{c,\lambda}^{-1}\bigl(z_{c}(h)-\mu_{c,y}\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">we define uncertainty score through the relative distance to successful and failed references:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{c}(h)=d_{c,\textup{{Pass}}}^{2}(h)-d_{c,\textup{{Fail}}}^{2}(h)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Pass</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Fail</mtext></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{c}(h)=d_{c,\textup{{Pass}}}^{2}(h)-d_{c,\textup{{Fail}}}^{2}(h).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">A larger score indicates greater relative proximity to failed references. We use <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> for initialization and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> for runtime action monitoring, selecting <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> for each model backbone and channel by task-grouped cross-validated AUROC (detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Representations and Estimator Fitting ‣ Appendix A Method and Formulation Details ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Interpretation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The design of our score was largely motivated by distance-based out-of-distribution detection literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller and Hein, 2025</a>)</cite>, but with careful customization for better fit in step-level agent uncertainty estimation. Unlike the relative Mahalanobis distance of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al. (2021)</a></cite>, which subtracts a class-agnostic background distance, we subtract the distance to the opposite outcome to capture a sharp delta signal of failure. Note that the Gaussian fitting only requires per-outcome means and a singular value decomposition, without gradient-based training, and can be iterated as the bank grows through multiple rounds of experience <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Escalation gates.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the measure of uncertainty, we define escalation gates for each uncertainty channel. Two channels address different sources of uncertainty: ambiguity in task specification and failure likelihood across stacked interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>. The initial query-level routing can identify tasks beyond the weak agent’s capability in advance, but cannot anticipate every difficulty encountered during runtime execution. Therefore, we combine an initial escalation gate, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g_{0}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{q}(h_{0})&gt;\tau_{q}\bigr\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{q}(h_{0})&gt;\tau_{q}\bigr\}</annotation></semantics></math>
which routes when <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, with a runtime escalation gate, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g_{t}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{a}(h_{t})&gt;\tau_{a}\bigr\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{a}(h_{t})&gt;\tau_{a}\bigr\}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math> that monitors each action of tasks retained by the initial gate given calibrated thresholds <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Runtime escalation occurs immediately after the first action with <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}=1</annotation></semantics></math>; The strong agent then receives the instruction, current screenshot, and recent steps run by the weak agent, and keeps control until the task termination (See Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for details).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Calibrating gating threshold to an escalation budget.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We set each threshold to a quantile of uncertainty scores on the reference tasks, so that each gate escalates a target fraction of tasks used to construct the representation bank. Let <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> be the target fraction of tasks escalated at initialization and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{esc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>esc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{esc}}</annotation></semantics></math> the target overall escalation rate. Since the runtime gate only monitors the tasks that the initial gate leaves to the weak agent, it should escalate a fraction <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{a}=(p_{\mathrm{esc}}-p_{q})/(1-p_{q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>esc</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{a}=(p_{\mathrm{esc}}-p_{q})/(1-p_{q})</annotation></semantics></math> of them, so that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{q}+(1-p_{q})p_{a}=p_{\mathrm{esc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>esc</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{q}+(1-p_{q})p_{a}=p_{\mathrm{esc}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The thresholds are then expressed as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{q}=Q_{1-p_{q}}\bigl(\{u_{q}(h_{i,0})\}_{i}\bigr),\qquad\tau_{a}=Q_{1-p_{a}}\bigl(\{U_{i}:u_{q}(h_{i,0})\leq\tau_{q}\}\bigr)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{q}=Q_{1-p_{q}}\bigl(\{u_{q}(h_{i,0})\}_{i}\bigr),\qquad\tau_{a}=Q_{1-p_{a}}\bigl(\{U_{i}:u_{q}(h_{i,0})\leq\tau_{q}\}\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> is the empirical <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>-quantile over reference tasks and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}=\max_{1\leq t\leq T_{i}}u_{a}(h_{i,t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}=\max_{1\leq t\leq T_{i}}u_{a}(h_{i,t})</annotation></semantics></math> is the maximum runtime score of the <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th reference trajectory of length <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. Intuitively, a fraction <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> of the reference tasks have initial scores above <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>, and among the tasks kept by the initial gate, a fraction <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> have a maximum runtime score above <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Note that we target escalation rates rather than failure probabilities because the gates only use the ranking of the scores. We compute <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> from each task’s maximum score because a single step above <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is enough for handoff; a quantile over individual steps would typically escalate more tasks than targeted.
All scores in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In Calibrating gating threshold to an escalation budget. ‣ 3.3 Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation ‣ 3 Method ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) are obtained out-of-fold from the same held-out reference set. After the thresholds are fixed, we refit one final estimator per uncertainty channel on all tasks in this same reference set for evaluation. Because refitting slightly changes the score scale, the target escalation rates are only approximate; we therefore report realized rates and match random baselines to them (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Task Success and Inference Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Reference Banks and Threshold Calibration ‣ Appendix A Method and Formulation Details ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Post-Handoff Oversight and Intervention</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We note that the strong agent can also get stuck in repeated action loops or get lost in multi-turn interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laban et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. However, its hidden states are inaccessible, while verbalized confidence is often highly unreliable as an uncertainty signal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchhof et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Shadow oversight.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To handle this challenge, we repurpose the weak agent from an actor as a <em id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Shadow observer</em> of strong agent for continued post-handoff oversight. We append each executed strong-agent step to the weak model’s history in its own action format and query with the current observation every <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> steps (<math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=3</annotation></semantics></math> by default). Given that context, the weak model generates a candidate action, allowing us to extract shadow representation <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{\rm sh}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>sh</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{\rm sh}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> at the same action token position as the strong black-box agent. Assuming that a higher uncertainty from the weak model also indicates a greater difficulty for the strong agent on average <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kale et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we can use that representation for the runtime action uncertainty estimation again <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{\rm sh}=u_{a}\bigl(h^{\rm sh}_{t}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>sh</mi></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{\rm sh}=u_{a}\bigl(h^{\rm sh}_{t}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math>, to define the Shadow oversight gate <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g_{\rm sh}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{\rm sh}&gt;\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}\bigr\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\rm sh}=\mathbb{I}\bigl\{u_{\rm sh}&gt;\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}\bigr\}</annotation></semantics></math> given a threshold <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty-triggered intervention.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\mathrm{sh}}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\mathrm{sh}}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, we discard the strong agent’s pending action and trigger a reflection-based intervention, which prompts the strong model agent to reassess its own progress toward the task goal and choose a new action using higher reasoning effort. We set the threshold <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>sh</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mathrm{sh}}</annotation></semantics></math> to the 90th percentile of per-step reference scores of the action representation bank.
We allow at most six Shadow interventions per task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vasudev et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and terminate further intervention once two have altered the strong agent’s proposed action (Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Post-Handoff Oversight ‣ Appendix A Method and Formulation Details ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmark and agents.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our framework on OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. For the weak agent, we use four open-source model backbones: EvoCUA-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite>, Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni (30B-A3B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deshmukh et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3.8-27B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>)</cite>. For the strong agent that takes over the escalated task and the Manager agent that decomposes tasks into subgoals and verifies their completion, we use Claude Opus 5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026b</a>)</cite>.
We compare our uncertainty-based W2SE and oversight framework and the baseline against always-on Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>, which use those models for every task and every step. More detailed definitions, execution settings, and model identifiers are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Experimental Details ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report task success rate and mean inference cost per task.
Costs are estimated from recorded token usage at fixed reference prices, including weak agent, Manager, strong-executor, and monitoring calls when enabled. These estimates measure the token-priced inference cost of the overall workflow.
Cost coverage and accounting details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Experimental Details ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<em id="S4.T1.5.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Random</em> escalation routes a matched fraction of tasks to Opus 5 uniformly at random; success is averaged over 10,000 random allocations.
